name: scale_vert_vel_1.5
hypothesis: Scaling the vertical velocity input by 1.5 makes the policy perceive a faster descent, prompting earlier main‑engine braking to compensate for the weaker thrust, which should reduce fuel waste and improve landing return.

name: scale_vert_vel_0.8
hypothesis: Scaling the vertical velocity input down to 0.8 makes the policy perceive a slower descent, encouraging later main‑engine braking, which should reduce fuel consumption and increase return while still allowing a safe landing under weaker thrust.

name: scale_vert_vel_0.75
hypothesis: Scaling the vertical velocity input to 0.75 further reduces the perceived descent speed, causing the policy to delay main‑engine braking even more. This should better compensate for the weaker main thrust, increasing fuel efficiency and mean return while still achieving safe landings.

name: scale_horiz_vert_0.8
hypothesis: Scaling both horizontal and vertical velocity inputs to 0.8 reduces perceived speeds, causing the policy to delay both side‑engine and main‑engine thrust. This should save fuel and better match the weaker main thrust, increasing mean return while maintaining safe landings.

name: scale_vert_0.8_height_1.1
hypothesis: Scaling the vertical velocity down to 0.8 makes the policy think it is descending slower, while scaling the height up to 1.1 makes the policy think it is higher. Both changes should delay main‑engine braking further, conserving fuel and increasing mean return under the weaker main thrust.

name: scale_height_1.2
hypothesis: Scaling the height input up to 1.2 makes the policy think the lander is higher, delaying main‑engine activation further. This should conserve fuel and increase mean return under the weaker main thrust while still achieving safe landings.

name: scale_vert_0.85_height_1.1
hypothesis: Scaling vertical velocity to 0.85 (making descent appear slightly slower) while scaling height to 1.1 (making the lander appear higher) should delay main‑engine braking just enough to conserve fuel under the weaker thrust, while still providing sufficient braking to land safely, potentially improving mean return over the 0.8 + 1.1 scaling.

name: scale_horiz_0.9_vert_0.8_height_1.1
hypothesis: Scaling horizontal velocity down to 0.9 reduces perceived side speed, leading to less side‑engine firing and fuel savings, while scaling vertical velocity to 0.8 and height to 1.1 delays main‑engine braking appropriately for the weaker thrust. Together these should increase mean return under weak_main physics.

name: scale_horiz_0.85_vert_0.8_height_1.1
hypothesis: Scaling horizontal velocity down to 0.85 reduces perceived side speed, leading to less side‑engine usage and fuel savings, while keeping vertical velocity at 0.8 and height at 1.1 to delay main‑engine braking appropriately for the weaker thrust. This should increase mean return over the previous best scaling.

name: scale_angle_0.9_vert_0.8_height_1.1_horiz_0.9
hypothesis: Scaling the body angle input to 0.9 reduces perceived tilt, leading to less side‑engine usage for attitude correction while keeping vertical velocity at 0.8, height at 1.1, and horizontal velocity at 0.9. This should save fuel and increase mean return under weak_main physics.

name: scale_vert_0.78_height_1.1_horiz_0.9_angle_0.9
hypothesis: Reducing the vertical velocity scaling to 0.78 further delays main‑engine braking, saving more fuel while still allowing safe landings under the weaker main thrust, potentially increasing mean return.

name: scale_x_angle_0.9_vert_0.78_height_1.1_horiz_0.9_angvel_0.9
hypothesis: Scaling the horizontal position (x) and angular velocity inputs down to 0.9 reduces perceived offset and rotation, leading to less side‑engine thrust for lateral correction and less attitude correction, while keeping height scaled up to 1.1, vertical velocity scaled to 0.78, horizontal velocity to 0.9, and body angle to 0.9. This should save fuel and increase mean return under the weaker main thrust without sacrificing safe landings.
